meta.description: Not Joseph Campbell. The exact line was an anonymous saying quoted in The Boston Post in July 1895 — and it is absent from Myths to Live By.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'If you walk far enough you'll meet yourself'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Joseph Campbell. Quote Investigator traced the wording to an anonymous saying in The Boston Post, 11 July 1895 — nine years before he was born.

answer.label: Not Joseph Campbell — an anonymous saying from the 1890s
answer.sourceLine: The exact wording was already a stock saying when a Massachusetts woman quoted it in The Boston Post in July 1895, nine years before Campbell was born. Quote Investigator ↗ found no substantive support for the Campbell ascription, and searched Myths to Live By — the book the internet credit names — without finding the line.

source.heading: Where the wording actually shows up first

docMeta.dd: 11 July 1895 · p. 3, col. 2 — column “Among the Women: Other Expressions”
Vina Howland of Oakland, Massachusetts, quoting an unnamed source (“the story they tell”)
Myths to Live By (Joseph Campbell, Viking Press, 1972) — quotation absent

source.excerpt: Miss Vina Howland of Oakland is a very pretty girl. She said: “How disappointed we were not to have this convention, but just think! I’ve seen Boston and convention, too; it’s like a dream. But ain’t it an awful place to get lost? I believe now the story they tell that is, ‘If you walk far enough you’ll meet yourself.’”
trail: A year earlier, a columnist in the Western Mail of Cardiff, Wales (4 August 1894) recorded a friend’s warning against revisiting a place of past happiness: “you will meet yourself, your past self, and it will not be good for you.” Cited and transcribed by Quote Investigator ↗ as a related, non-time-travel use.

The exact eight-word form appears in The Boston Post on 11 July 1895, and the joke keeps resurfacing — Honolulu’s crooked streets in 1914, circular roads in Illinois in 1916, Boston city planning in The North American Review in 1920. All documented in QI’s chronology ↗.
The Campbell credit is traceable to a Goodreads quotation page ↗ pointing at Myths to Live By; QI checked that book against scans and the line is not in it.

Campbell’s own sourced record backs this up: Wikiquote’s Joseph Campbell page ↗, which cites The Hero with a Thousand Faces, The Power of Myth, Pathways to Bliss and others and keeps a Disputed section, contains no version of this line.
source.excerptNote: Transcribed by Quote Investigator ↗ from The Boston Post, 11 July 1895, p. 3. Note that the speaker introduces it as a saying already in circulation, not as her own line.

source.rightsNote: The eight-word saying has no known author and its earliest documented printing is The Boston Post of 11 July 1895 — comfortably before 1931, so both the saying and that printing are in the public domain in the United States. The later reworkings are not: Marion Woodman’s 1982 sentence, Pratchett and Briggs’s 1994 Discworld Companion entry and David Mitchell’s 2004 Cloud Atlas passphrase all remain in copyright to their authors and publishers.

author.name: Joseph Campbell
author.kicker: The name it got pinned to
author.heading: Why the quote landed on Campbell
author.bio: Joseph Campbell taught literature at Sarah Lawrence College from 1934 to 1972 and built a career out of finding the same story shape under the myths of every culture — the argument of The Hero with a Thousand Faces (1949) and of the posthumous PBS series The Power of Myth, first broadcast in 1988. That reputation as the man who explains journeys is exactly why travel-shaped aphorisms drift toward his name. This one drifted the whole way: it is a nineteenth-century folk saying about getting lost in Boston, and it appears in none of his documented work.

cite.sourceCitation: Earliest documented in “Among the Women: Other Expressions,” The Boston Post (Boston, MA), July 11, 1895, p. 3, col. 2, quoted in Garson O’Toole, “Quote Origin: If You Walk Far Enough You’ll Meet Yourself,” Quote Investigator, November 19, 2022. Originator anonymous; not found in the work of Joseph Campbell.

misattribution.heading: Four names on one saying — and none of them wrote it
misattribution.intro: This is a folk saying with an unusually crowded credit line. Quote Investigator opens its investigation by listing Terry Pratchett, Marion Woodman, Joseph Campbell, David Mitchell and Vina Howland as candidates; the documented answer is none of them.

items.scope: “If you travel far enough, you’ll eventually meet yourself.”
items.why: The credit rests on a Goodreads entry ↗ citing Myths to Live By, with comments dating to January 2016. Quote Investigator searched that book against scans and reports the quotation is absent ↗, and found no substantive support for the ascription. Wikiquote’s Campbell page ↗ carries no version of it either.

items.scope: “If you travel far enough, one day you will recognize yourself coming down the road to meet yourself.”
items.why: The Canadian Jungian analyst used this expanded form in Addiction to Perfection ↗ (Inner City Books, 1982) — and it is her wording that a 1993 traveller’s quotation anthology reprinted, correctly credited to her. It is a reworking of a saying already long in print, not the source.

items.scope: “Walk far enough and you will meet yourself, coming the other way.”
items.why: This is an entry about the caves of Lancre in The Discworld Companion (Victor Gollancz, 1994), co-written with Stephen Briggs. Quote Investigator places it in the chain of later users ↗, not at its head.
A secret passphrase in the Sonmi~451 section of Cloud Atlas (Sceptre, 2004). Documented by QI as a use, not an origin ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: Quote Investigator’s conclusion ↗: the saying was circulating by 1895, the originator remains anonymous, and the linkage to Joseph Campbell is currently unsupported.

context.heading: A joke about Boston’s streets, not a lesson about the soul
lead: Read as spiritual advice, the line sounds like Campbell: go far enough into the journey and the thing you find is yourself. Read in its earliest documented setting it is a gag about municipal planning. In The Boston Post of 11 July 1895, a visitor named Vina Howland of Oakland, Massachusetts was complaining about how easy Boston is to get lost in, and reached for a saying she clearly expected her listener to know already — “the story they tell.” Quote Investigator ↗ tracks the same joke through crooked streets in Honolulu in 1914, circular roads in Illinois in 1916, and Boston again in The North American Review in 1920, alongside a separate strand about hats so fashionable you keep running into copies of your own.

The mystical reading is real, but it arrived later and from other pens. The Jungian analyst Marion Woodman gave the saying its self-discovery turn in Addiction to Perfection in 1982; Terry Pratchett and Stephen Briggs made it a property of magic caves in The Discworld Companion in 1994; David Mitchell used a clipped form as a passphrase in Cloud Atlas in 2004. None of them is the originator, and none of them is Campbell.
context.detailsSummary: Campbell as a quotation magnet — and the cases that went the other way
detailsBody: Campbell attracts unsourced aphorisms in bulk, and the honest answer differs case by case — often in his favour. Quote Investigator’s investigation of the line about getting rid of the life you planned ↗ finds that one genuinely his, recorded by Diane K. Osbon in A Joseph Campbell Companion (1991) and only later drifting to E. M. Forster, a credit QI calls spurious. Its investigation of “the cave you fear to enter holds the treasure you seek” ↗ likewise concludes that that one did originate with Campbell, in a longer form later compressed by others.

So the test is not “does it sound like him.” It is whether a documented page exists. For the cave line there is one. For “if you walk far enough you’ll meet yourself,” the documented page is a Boston newspaper from 1895, and Campbell is nowhere near it.
context.pull: “I believe now the story they tell” — in 1895 it was already the story they tell.

sourcesVerified.claim: Quote Investigator's earliest close match is The Boston Post, 11 July 1895, p. 3, col. 2, quoting Vina Howland of Oakland, Massachusetts: "I believe now the story they tell that is, 'If you walk far enough you'll meet yourself.'" QI concludes the originator remains anonymous, has not found substantive support for the Joseph Campbell ascription, searched Myths to Live By (Viking Press, 1972) and found the quotation absent, and documents the 1894 Western Mail (Cardiff) item, Marion Woodman's 1982 Addiction to Perfection p.129 wording, Pratchett & Briggs's 1994 Discworld Companion p.138 wording, David Mitchell's 2004 Cloud Atlas p.336 passphrase, plus the 1914 Argos Reflector, 1916 Daily Advocate and 1920 North American Review instances.
Goodreads hosts a quotation page reading "If you travel far enough, you'll eventually meet yourself." credited to Joseph Campbell, Myths to Live By.

Wikiquote's Joseph Campbell page gives his dates as 26 March 1904 - 30 October 1987, has sections for The Hero with a Thousand Faces (1949), The Power of Myth (1988), Pathways to Bliss (2004) and a Disputed section, and contains no quotation with the words "far enough" anywhere on the page.

Joseph Campbell (March 26, 1904 - October 30, 1987) was an American professor of literature at Sarah Lawrence College from 1934 to 1972; The Hero with a Thousand Faces was published in 1949 and Myths to Live By in 1972; the PBS series The Power of Myth with Bill Moyers was first broadcast in 1988, the year after his death.
Myths to Live By was published by Viking Press in New York in 1972 and consists of essays originally given as lectures at the Cooper Union Forum between 1958 and 1971.
The Internet Archive hosts a scanned copy of Joseph Campbell's Myths to Live By (Arkana edition, originally Viking Press 1972).
The Internet Archive hosts a scanned copy of Marion Woodman's Addiction to Perfection: The Still Unravished Bride: A Psychological Study, Inner City, Toronto, 1982.

Quote Investigator's separate investigation of "The cave you fear to enter holds the treasure you seek" concludes that QI believes the expression did originate with Joseph Campbell, possibly in a longer version telescoped by others.

Quote Investigator's investigation of "We must be willing to get rid of the life we've planned, so as to have the life that is waiting for us" credits the statement to Joseph Campbell via Diane K. Osbon, who stated in her 1991 book A Joseph Campbell Companion: Reflections on the Art of Living that she recorded Campbell's words in her journals, and concludes that the linkage to E. M. Forster appears to be spurious.
